extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of classical literature; listeners of a university lecture on Greek genius
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for assessing the character, style, and merits of major Greek authors (Homer, Pindar, Aeschylus, Herodotus, Sophocles, Euripides, Thucydides, Aristophanes) and for judging historical and poetic composition more generally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical fidelity / minute description (Homer)
rubrics_metrics.description: Homer displays an almost historical fidelity in the description of incidents the most minute; he is a 'faithful voucher' (Homeros) and an unfalsifying witness of the true shape and fashion of heroic life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value poems that preserve detailed, seemingly factual depictions of incidents and social forms; treat Homeric detail as poetic truth rather than literal blindness or simple invention. Anti-pattern: dismissing such detail as mere later fabrication or reducing it to the 'blind man' legend.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internal vision / poetic inward sight (Milton, Ossian)
rubrics_metrics.description: Great poets (e.g., Milton, Ossian) may 'see' with the internal eye of the mind even while deprived of external light; their poetry is clothed in an inward, often melancholy, twilight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess poetic imagination by its power to produce vivid inner vision and emotional atmosphere independent of literal visual experience. Recognize melancholy or twilight tones as signs of inward perception rather than physical defect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commingling of past marvels and present circumstances (Homer)
rubrics_metrics.description: Homer's compositions place two worlds together — the world of marvels and tradition and the living circumstances and present concerns of the poet — and this commingling lends a characteristic charm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Praise works that fuse mythic/traditional elements with contemporary detail, using the past to adorn and the present to illustrate; value balance between the marvelous and the immediate human context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetic role in preserving heroic social forms
rubrics_metrics.description: Epic poetry can represent an age in transition, preserving heroic forms (kings claiming descent from heroic races) even as society becomes more prosaic and republican.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating epic or heroic poetry, note whether it preserves the ethos and institutions of an earlier age and whether it conveys the social transformation that surrounds its composition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pindaric loftiness, musical softness, and dignified perspective
rubrics_metrics.description: Pindar's peculiar characteristics are the lofty beauty and musical softness of his language, and his fondness for considering every subject in the most dignified point of view.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value elevated diction, musicality, and the habit of treating subjects in a dignified manner; expect festival odes to celebrate victors, ancestral lineage, cities, or deities with stately tone. Anti-pattern: modern imitations that substitute elaborate wildness or artificial obscurity for Pindar's native elevation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obscurity from local allusion (Pindar)
rubrics_metrics.description: Any obscurity in Pindar arises from frequent allusions to things foreign to us but familiar to his original audience (e.g., local myths, customs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between genuine poetic obscurity caused by cultural/contextual references and obscurity arising from affectation; translations/editions should annotate rather than 'clean up' such references.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form and function of festival/lyric songs (Pindar)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pindar's festival songs are heroic or epic poems composed in celebration of particular events, accompanied with music and dancing and brought forward somewhat dramatically; they bear little resemblance to modern lyric as commonly understood.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When classifying or composing 'lyric' festival pieces, account for their ceremonial, musical, and occasionally dramatic function; expect narrative celebration rather than introspective lyricism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aeschylean tragic power and moral sublimity
rubrics_metrics.description: Aeschylus is warlike, bold, and lofty; his poetry is pre-eminently powerful in the expression of the terrible and tragic passions, combining deep poetic feeling with intense earnestness of philosophic thought; he presents a universal recurrence to a world of tragedy (e.g., subjection of old gods, decline of greatness).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value tragedy that attains moral sublimity and seriousness of thought beyond mere poetic beauty; favour breadth of theme (cosmic decline, moral catastrophe) and sustained tragic vision rather than isolated sensational events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Herodotean qualities for historical writing
rubrics_metrics.description: Herodotus's history is characterized by truth, simplicity, clearness, flexibility, and unsought pathos; he interweaves episodes and travel-observations into a candid narration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For historical composition, prize candid narration, readable clarity, humane observation, and flexible arrangement that allows episodic material and cultural description; treat these as the model for 'perfect in its kind' historical writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sophoclean transparency, internal harmony, and balance
rubrics_metrics.description: Sophocles exhibits transparent beauty, internal harmony and the sign of perfection of form and language; his work occupies the middle region between sublime wonder and common life where poetry is most favorable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value works that balance grandeur and human tenderness, that achieve lucid beauty and structural perfection; aim for a middle ground between supernatural exaltation and mundane detail for the highest poetic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Euripidean oratorical/sophistic influence as a stylistic trait
rubrics_metrics.description: Euripides was as much an orator as a poet and borrowed ornaments from the school of sophistry, producing effects considered foreign to pure poetry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating verse-drama, note the presence of rhetorical or sophistic ornamentation: it may enrich argument but can be judged as divergent from classical poetic purity. Consider context and audience when assessing appropriateness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corrupting influence of sophistry on taste and art
rubrics_metrics.description: The rise of sophists and sophistry acquired wide, destructive influence over the intellectual character of Greece and contributed to the decay and ruin of art and genius.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critically watch for sophistic tendencies (deceptive subtlety, form over substance) that may erode poetic integrity; favour returns to robust ethical and aesthetic standards (e.g., Socratic/Platonic corrective).

rubrics_metrics.name: Thucydidean method for historical/narrative power
rubrics_metrics.description: Thucydides' method consists firstly in interweaving political speeches to reveal secret motives and councils; secondly in almost poetical, minute, energetic representations of battles and external incidents; and thirdly in accumulation of the highest excellencies of style — rich, ornamented, and energetic prose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value histories that deploy reconstructed speeches to disclose motives, vivid battlefield narrative, and elevated, energetic prose. Be mindful that such a massive, ambitious style can verge on hardness or obscurity — possibly suited to dark subject-matter but risky if it impedes clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modern historical preference: brevity and precision
rubrics_metrics.description: Modern historians prefer short and precise sketches which carry us without circumlocution to the point, explaining events as they happened with true causes, rather than minute poetical descriptions of battles and sieges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In contemporary historical composition, prioritize concision, causal explanation, and economy of narrative over elaborate poetical detail; match descriptive depth to the needs of modern readers and the accumulation of available facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextual judgement of comic and popular forms (Aristophanes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristophanes must be judged by being transplanted into his age: the old comedy's licence (Bacchic festivals) permitted wildness, but the true poet still maintained elegance of language and versification and a sense of poetical dignity amid extravagance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate popular/comic drama with attention to its social/ceremonial context; allow greater freedom of fancy, but still require poetic craft, linguistic elegance, and evidence that extravagance is not mere coarseness or personal spite. Anti-pattern: condemning or excising forms solely because of obscenity without attending to poetic merit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate inclusion of feminine tenderness and avoidance of vulgarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Greek literature often lacks a delicate bloom of womanly tenderness (due in part to social seclusion of women), and where that tenderness is absent we sometimes miss it; conversely, vulgarity or coarseness in its place is detestable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When composing or judging literature, consider whether inclusion of humane, tender female perspectives would improve the work; avoid gratuitous coarseness and the false introduction of 'womanly tenderness' as affectation. Assess whether social context explains omissions but does not excuse poor moral taste.
